column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Which of these cells is a gamete?
column14: A skin cell
column15: A sperm cell
column28: Gametes are sex cells: sperm and eggs. Skin, muscle, and white blood cells are somatic (body) cells. A common mistake is thinking any cell in the body can be a gamete.
column29: Gametes are the cells that join together at fertilization.

column9: Cells that make up the body, such as skin, bone, and muscle cells, are called ___ cells.
column28: Body cells are somatic cells. They are diploid and are made by mitosis. A common mistake is writing germ cells, which are the cells in reproductive organs that go through meiosis.
column29: This is the word paired with 'gamete' when you sort the two main groups of cells in your body.

column9: A cell that has two complete sets of chromosomes, one set from each parent, is called
column14: haploid
column15: diploid
column28: Diploid (2n) means two sets of chromosomes, like your body cells. Haploid means only one set. A common mistake is mixing up the two words; remember di- means two.
column29: The prefix di- means two.

column9: Which symbol do biologists use for the haploid number of chromosomes?
column14: 2n
column15: n
column28: The haploid number is written n (one set). The diploid number is written 2n (two sets). A common mistake is picking 2n, which is the body-cell number.
column29: Haploid cells have one set of chromosomes, so the symbol has no number in front.

column9: In a flowering plant, such as an apple tree, where does meiosis take place?
column14: In the anthers and ovules of the flower
column15: In the leaves
column16: In the growing tips of the roots
column17: In the xylem of the stem
column28: Meiosis happens only in reproductive parts. In a flower, that is the anthers (pollen) and the ovules (eggs). Root tips and leaves grow by mitosis, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Meiosis is for making reproductive cells. Which plant parts are used for reproduction?

column9: How many times does the cell divide during meiosis?
column14: Once
column15: Twice
column28: Meiosis has two divisions: meiosis I and meiosis II. A common mistake is answering four, which is the number of cells made, not the number of divisions.
column29: The process has two parts, named with Roman numerals.

column9: A germ cell in a bull's testis finishes both meiosis I and meiosis II. How many sperm cells can it produce?
column28: One cell divides into 2 in meiosis I, and each of those divides again in meiosis II: 2 × 2 = 4 sperm. A common mistake is answering 2, which is what mitosis makes.
column29: Count the cells after the first division, then let each of them divide again.

column9: A sperm cell joins with an egg cell. What is this event called?
column14: Meiosis
column15: Fertilization
column28: Fertilization is when a sperm and an egg join. Meiosis is the process that made the sperm and egg earlier, which is the common mix-up.
column29: This is the event that starts a new organism, not the process that made the sex cells.

column9: The single diploid cell formed when a sperm fertilizes an egg is called a ___.
column28: The zygote is the first cell of a new organism. It is diploid because it has a set of chromosomes from each gamete. A common mistake is calling it a gamete, but gametes are the haploid cells that joined.
column29: This word starts the life of every baby, puppy, or calf. It is one cell that will divide by mitosis.

column9: What are homologous chromosomes?
column14: Two chromosomes of a matching pair, one from each parent, that carry the same genes
column15: Two identical copies of one chromosome joined at a centromere
column16: Only the X and Y chromosomes
column17: Chromosomes that are found only in gametes
column28: Homologous chromosomes are a matching pair: one from mom, one from dad, same genes in the same order. Two identical copies joined at a centromere are sister chromatids, the most common mix-up.
column29: Think of a pair of shoes: one came from each parent.

column9: Which words describe a human skin cell and a human egg cell, in that order?
column14: Diploid, haploid
column15: Haploid, diploid
column28: A skin cell is a body cell with 46 chromosomes (diploid). An egg is a gamete with 23 (haploid). A common mistake is calling the egg diploid because it is a large cell; size does not set chromosome number.
column29: Which cell has 46 chromosomes and which has 23?

column9: You have 46 chromosomes in each body cell. Where did they come from?
column14: All 46 came from your mother
column15: 23 came from your mother and 23 from your father
column17: Each parent gave a random number that adds to 46
column28: Each gamete has 23 chromosomes, one from each pair, so the egg gave 23 and the sperm gave 23. A common mistake is thinking the mother gives more because the egg is bigger.
column29: Each parent gives one gamete, and each gamete has half the body-cell number.

column9: A student's model shows two matching chromosomes wrapped tightly together, trading pieces. Which phase does the model show?
column14: Prophase I
column15: Metaphase II
column28: Homologous chromosomes pair up and trade pieces (crossing over) in prophase I. In meiosis II the partners have already separated, so they cannot trade, which is why the II phases are wrong.
column29: The matching partners have to be together for this to happen. When are they paired up?

column9: When homologous chromosomes trade matching segments of DNA, the event is called ___.
column20: crossing over|crossing-over|crossover|cross over|crossing over of chromosomes
column28: Crossing over swaps pieces between homologous chromosomes, giving each chromosome a new mix of genes. A common mistake is calling it independent assortment, which is about how the pairs line up, not swapping pieces.
column29: Two chromosomes 'cross' each other and swap parts.

column9: What are the cells in the ovaries and testes that go through meiosis called?
column14: Germ cells
column15: Somatic cells
column28: Germ cells are the cells in reproductive organs that undergo meiosis to make gametes. Somatic cells are ordinary body cells, the common mistake.
column29: These are the cells that 'germinate' the next generation.

column9: Corn leaf cells have 20 chromosomes. Meiosis takes place in the corn plant's flowers. How many chromosomes does each cell made by meiosis have?
column28: Meiosis halves the chromosome number: 20 ÷ 2 = 10. A common mistake is doubling to 40, or dividing by 4 because 4 cells are made.
column29: Meiosis cuts the chromosome number in half, once.

column9: How many pairs of chromosomes are in a human body cell?
column28: 46 chromosomes make 23 pairs. A common mistake is answering 46, which is the number of chromosomes, not pairs.
column29: Each pair has 2 chromosomes. How many pairs make 46?

column9: The X and Y chromosomes, which decide whether a person is male or female, are called ___ chromosomes.
column28: X and Y are the sex chromosomes. The other 22 pairs are autosomes. A common mistake is calling them homologous; X and Y are a pair, but the term for them is sex chromosomes.
column29: They determine the sex of a person.

column9: A human male's body cells are XY. Which sex chromosome can one of his sperm cells carry?
column14: Only X
column15: Only Y
column28: Meiosis separates the X and Y, so each sperm gets one: about half carry X and half carry Y. A common mistake is thinking every sperm carries Y because the father is male.
column29: In meiosis, each pair is split up, and each gamete gets just one member of the pair.

column9: Which of these is a haploid cell?
column14: A human liver cell
column15: A human egg cell
column28: An egg is a gamete with one set of chromosomes, so it is haploid. Liver and nerve cells are diploid body cells, and a zygote is diploid because two gametes joined. The zygote is the common wrong choice.
column29: Which cell was made by meiosis and is waiting to join another cell?

column9: Every normal egg cell made by a human female carries an X chromosome.
column28: True. A female's cells are XX, so whichever one an egg gets, it is an X. The sperm decides the baby's sex. A common mistake is thinking the egg can carry a Y.
column29: What are a female's two sex chromosomes?

column9: Which phase comes right after metaphase I?
column14: Anaphase I
column15: Prophase II
column28: Each division goes prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. So metaphase I is followed by anaphase I. A common mistake is jumping to meiosis II before meiosis I is finished.
column29: PMAT: the order is the same in each division.

column9: Put the phases of meiosis I in order.
column14: Anaphase I
column15: Prophase I
column28: Prophase I → metaphase I → anaphase I → telophase I (PMAT). A common mistake is swapping metaphase and anaphase; the chromosomes must line up before they are pulled apart.
column29: Remember PMAT.

column9: In a pipe-cleaner model, a student pulls the two identical halves of each chromosome toward opposite ends of the cell. Which phase is she modeling?
column14: Anaphase I
column15: Anaphase II
column28: The two identical halves are sister chromatids, and they separate in anaphase II. In anaphase I, the homologous pairs separate and sister chromatids stay together, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Identical halves means sister chromatids. Which division splits those?

column9: Before meiosis begins, each chromosome is copied. The two identical copies, held together at the centromere, are called sister ___.
column28: The two copies are sister chromatids. They separate in meiosis II. A common mistake is calling them homologous chromosomes, which are a pair from two different parents.
column29: The word starts with 'chromat-' like chromosome.

column9: When is the DNA copied for meiosis?
column14: During interphase (S phase), before meiosis I
column15: Between meiosis I and meiosis II
column17: The DNA is never copied for meiosis
column28: DNA is copied once, in the S phase of interphase, before meiosis I. There is no copying between meiosis I and II, which is the common mistake; that is why the number ends up halved.
column29: DNA is copied before the cell starts dividing, the same as for mitosis.

column9: You cut your finger, and over a week new skin cells fill the cut. Which process made those new skin cells?
column14: Mitosis
column15: Meiosis
column28: Growth and repair use mitosis, which makes identical diploid cells. Meiosis only makes gametes in the reproductive organs, the common mix-up.
column29: Are skin cells gametes or body cells?

column9: Match each human cell count to its number.
column14: Chromosomes in a human body cell :: 46
column15: Chromosomes in a human gamete :: 23
column16: Sex chromosomes in a human gamete :: 1
column28: Body cells have 46. Gametes have half, 23: 22 autosomes plus 1 sex chromosome. A common mistake is thinking a gamete keeps both sex chromosomes.
column29: Start with 46 for the body cell, then halve it for the gamete.

column9: A litter of puppies has the same two parents, yet the puppies look different from each other. What is the main reason?
column14: Each puppy got a different mix of genes, because meiosis makes every sperm and egg different
column15: Each puppy was made by mitosis from one parent
column16: Puppies get all their genes from the mother
column17: Each puppy has a different number of chromosomes
column28: Meiosis shuffles chromosomes, so every gamete carries a different mix of the parents' genes. Different gametes made each puppy. A common mistake is thinking siblings should be identical because they share parents.
column29: Think about the sperm and egg that made each puppy. Were they all the same?

column9: In which phase do chromosomes line up single file across the middle of each of two cells?
column14: Metaphase I
column15: Metaphase II
column28: In metaphase II, the two cells from meiosis I each line up their chromosomes single file. In metaphase I, chromosomes line up in pairs inside one cell, which is the common mix-up.
column29: There are already two cells, so meiosis I is over.

column9: When meiosis I is finished, how many cells are there?
column28: Meiosis I splits one cell into 2. Meiosis II then splits each of those, giving 4. A common mistake is answering 4 before the second division has happened.
column29: Meiosis I is only the first of two divisions.

column9: Which of these are gametes? Select all that apply.
column14: A human sperm cell
column15: A frog egg cell, before fertilization
column28: Sperm and egg cells are gametes, in any animal. Skin and liver cells are body cells. A zygote forms when two gametes join, so it is no longer a gamete; that is the common wrong pick.
column29: Look for sex cells: sperm and eggs.

column9: Why do gametes need to be haploid?
column14: So that when two gametes join, the zygote has the normal diploid number
column15: So that gametes can divide by mitosis faster
column16: So that gametes are identical to the parent cell
column17: So that the zygote has half the normal number
column28: A haploid egg plus a haploid sperm makes a diploid zygote, so the chromosome number stays the same each generation. A common mistake is thinking the zygote ends up with half.
column29: What happens to the number when two gametes add together?

column9: Sperm cells and egg cells are made by a type of cell division called ___.
column28: Meiosis makes gametes. A common mistake is writing mitosis, which makes body cells for growth and repair.
column29: It is not the division your skin uses to heal.

column9: A chimpanzee has 48 chromosomes in its body cells. How many chromosomes are in a chimpanzee egg cell?
column28: An egg is haploid: 48 ÷ 2 = 24. A common mistake is answering 48, forgetting that meiosis halves the number.
column29: Meiosis cuts the body-cell number in half.

column9: Each egg cell of a garden pea plant has 7 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in one of its leaf cells?
column28: Leaf cells are diploid, double the egg: 7 × 2 = 14. A common mistake is halving again to get 3.5; going from gamete to body cell means doubling.
column29: Is a leaf cell haploid or diploid? Go the other way from meiosis.

column9: A baby rabbit's zygote had 44 chromosomes. How many of them came from the father's sperm?
column28: Each parent's gamete gives half: 44 ÷ 2 = 22 from the sperm and 22 from the egg. A common mistake is thinking the sperm gave all 44.
column29: Two gametes added together make the zygote.

column9: Which example is sexual reproduction, which depends on meiosis?
column14: A strawberry plant sending out runners that root into new plants
column15: A sea star regrowing a whole body from a broken arm
column16: A white-tailed deer fawn born to a doe and a buck
column17: A bacterium splitting into two cells
column28: The fawn came from a sperm (buck) and an egg (doe), both made by meiosis. Runners, regrowth, and splitting use only one parent and make copies, which is asexual reproduction.
column29: Look for the example with two parents.

column9: A house mouse cell has 40 chromosomes before meiosis begins. How many homologous pairs does it have?
column28: Each homologous pair has 2 chromosomes: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 pairs. A common mistake is answering 40, which counts chromosomes, not pairs.
column29: A pair is two chromosomes.

column9: What does crossing over increase?
column14: Genetic variation
column15: The number of chromosomes
column28: Crossing over mixes genes between homologous chromosomes, so gametes are more varied. It does not change the chromosome number, which is a common mistake.
column29: Crossing over makes each chromosome a new mix of mom's and dad's genes.

column9: Put the phases of meiosis II in order.
column14: Telophase II
column15: Metaphase II
column28: Prophase II → metaphase II → anaphase II → telophase II, the same PMAT order as meiosis I. A common mistake is putting telophase before anaphase.
column29: PMAT works for meiosis II too.

column9: Which two chromosomes are a homologous pair?
column14: Chromosome 7 from your mother and chromosome 7 from your father
column15: Chromosome 7 and chromosome 8, both from your mother
column17: The two sister chromatids of chromosome 3
column28: Homologous chromosomes are the same chromosome number, one from each parent, carrying the same genes. Sister chromatids are copies of one chromosome, the common mix-up.
column29: A homologous pair is a match: same chromosome, different parents.

column9: Imagine human eggs and sperm were made by mitosis, so each had 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes would a zygote have?
column28: 46 + 46 = 92, and the number would double every generation. Meiosis prevents this by halving the number in gametes. A common mistake is answering 46 without adding the two gametes.
column29: A zygote gets all the chromosomes from both gametes.

column9: What is the job of the spindle fibers during meiosis?
column14: They pull chromosomes to opposite sides of the cell
column15: They copy the DNA
column28: Spindle fibers attach to chromosomes and pull them apart in anaphase, just as in mitosis. A common mistake is thinking they cause crossing over, which happens between the chromosomes themselves.
column29: Spindle fibers work like ropes.

column9: In a human male, where does the meiosis that makes sperm take place?
column14: In the testes
column15: In the heart
column28: Sperm are made by meiosis in the testes. Bone marrow makes blood cells by mitosis, a common wrong choice.
column29: Meiosis happens in reproductive organs.

column9: During anaphase I, what stays together?
column14: The two sister chromatids of each chromosome
column15: The two homologous chromosomes of each pair
column16: All the chromosomes that came from the mother
column28: In anaphase I, homologous pairs separate but each chromosome stays as two sister chromatids. The chromatids split later, in anaphase II. A common mistake is thinking the homologs stay together.
column29: Two different things separate in meiosis: one in meiosis I and one in meiosis II.

column9: Which description fits a normal human sperm cell?
column14: One chromosome from each of the 23 pairs, some originally from the man's mother and some from his father
column15: Two copies of every chromosome, 46 in all
column16: Only chromosomes the man inherited from his father
column28: A gamete gets one chromosome from every pair (23). Because pairs line up randomly, it gets a mix of the man's maternal and paternal chromosomes. A common mistake is thinking a man passes on only his father's chromosomes.
column29: Each gamete gets one from each pair. Which one from each pair is random.

column9: Which event happens in meiosis but NOT in mitosis?
column14: Homologous chromosomes pair up
column15: DNA is copied before the division
column28: Only meiosis pairs up homologous chromosomes (in prophase I). Both processes copy DNA, form spindles, and separate sister chromatids, so those are the common wrong choices.
column29: Three of these happen in both processes. Which one is special to making gametes?

column9: Which of these happen in BOTH mitosis and meiosis? Select all that apply.
column14: DNA is copied before the division starts
column15: Spindle fibers move the chromosomes
column17: Sister chromatids separate at some point
column18: The cells end up with half the chromosome number
column28: Both copy DNA first, use spindle fibers, and separate sister chromatids (anaphase in mitosis, anaphase II in meiosis). Crossing over and halving happen only in meiosis, the common wrong picks.
column29: Cross out anything that is about pairing up homologs or making gametes.

column9: Match each phase of meiosis I to what happens in it.
column14: Prophase I :: Homologous chromosomes pair up and cross over
column15: Metaphase I :: Homologous pairs line up at the middle of the cell
column16: Anaphase I :: Homologous chromosomes move to opposite sides
column17: Telophase I :: Two cells form, each with half the chromosome number
column28: Prophase I: pair and cross over. Metaphase I: pairs line up. Anaphase I: partners pulled apart. Telophase I: two haploid cells. A common mistake is putting the pairing in metaphase; pairing starts in prophase I.
column29: Use PMAT: prepare, middle, apart, two.

column9: A mosquito species has 6 chromosomes (3 homologous pairs) in its body cells. Ignoring crossing over, how many different chromosome combinations can its gametes have?
column28: Each pair can line up 2 ways, so the combinations are 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8. A common mistake is answering 6 (2 × 3) instead of multiplying 2 by itself 3 times.
column29: Each pair has 2 choices. Multiply the choices for every pair.

column9: A garden pea plant has 14 chromosomes in its body cells. When its homologous chromosomes pair up early in meiosis I, how many pairs form?
column28: Each group is one homologous pair, and 14 chromosomes make 14 ÷ 2 = 7 pairs. A common mistake is answering 14, counting chromosomes instead of pairs.
column29: How many pairs can 14 chromosomes make?

column9: About how many different chromosome combinations can independent assortment alone produce in one person's gametes?
column28: Each of the 23 pairs can line up 2 ways, so the combinations are 2²³ ≈ 8.4 million. A common mistake is squaring 23 instead of raising 2 to the 23rd power.
column29: Each pair gives 2 choices, and there are 23 pairs.

column9: After crossing over, what is true about a chromosome that took part?
column14: It carries a new mix of genes from both parents
column15: It is now identical to its homologous partner
column16: It has twice as many genes as before
column17: It is no longer part of a homologous pair
column28: Crossing over swaps matching segments, so the chromosome now has some of mom's genes and some of dad's. It has the same genes as before, just new combinations. A common mistake is thinking it gains extra genes.
column29: Pieces were swapped, not added.

column9: A student's model shows homologous pairs lined up at the center of a cell. In one pair the chromosome from mom is on the left; in the next pair the chromosome from mom is on the right. Which idea is the model showing?
column14: Independent assortment
column15: Crossing over
column28: Each pair lines up in a random direction in metaphase I, independent of the other pairs. That is independent assortment. Crossing over is the swapping of pieces, the common mix-up.
column29: Nothing is being swapped in this model. What is random about it?

column9: A scientist counts chromosomes in cells from a tomato flower. A parent cell has 24 chromosomes, and it divides into four cells with 12 chromosomes each. Which process happened?
column14: Meiosis
column15: Mitosis
column28: Four cells with half the number (24 → 12) is meiosis. Mitosis makes two cells with the same number (24 → 24), the common mix-up.
column29: Look at both clues: how many cells, and what happened to the number?

column9: A horse has 64 chromosomes in its body cells. Which list correctly gives the chromosome numbers in a horse's sperm, egg, and zygote?
column28: Sperm and egg are haploid (32 each), and the zygote adds them back to 64. A common mistake is calling the zygote haploid too.
column29: The zygote is what you get when you add the sperm and egg together.

column9: Put these events in the order they happen in a human life cycle.
column14: The zygote divides by mitosis to form an embryo
column15: Germ cells in the parents go through meiosis
column16: A sperm fertilizes an egg, forming a zygote
column17: The embryo grows into a baby whose body cells are all diploid
column28: Meiosis makes gametes → fertilization makes a zygote → mitosis makes the embryo → the baby grows. A common mistake is putting mitosis before fertilization; the zygote must exist before it can divide.
column29: You need gametes before fertilization, and a zygote before it can divide.

column9: Which statements explain why meiosis is important for sexual reproduction? Select all that apply.
column14: It keeps the chromosome number the same from one generation to the next
column15: It makes gametes that are genetically different from one another
column17: It makes exact copies of the parent
column18: It halves the chromosome number so fertilization restores the diploid number
column28: Meiosis halves the number so fertilization brings it back to normal, keeping it steady across generations, and it makes varied gametes. Repairing skin and making exact copies are jobs of mitosis, the common wrong picks.
column29: Two of these describe mitosis instead.

column9: Two parents have three children, and none of them are identical twins. Which two meiosis events best explain why the children are genetically different?
column14: Crossing over and independent assortment
column15: DNA copying and cytokinesis
column28: Crossing over mixes genes on chromosomes, and independent assortment mixes which chromosomes go into each gamete. Nondisjunction is an error, not a normal source of variety, which is the common trap.
column29: Which two events normally shuffle genes in every meiosis?

column9: When a homologous pair lies tightly together early in meiosis, the group of four chromatids is called a ___.
column28: Two homologous chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, make 4 chromatids: a tetrad (tetra- means four). A common mistake is calling it a centromere, which is just the spot that holds sister chromatids together.
column29: The prefix tetra- means four.

column9: Which cell has the same number of chromosomes as a human gamete?
column14: A cell at the end of meiosis I
column15: A cell at the start of prophase I
column17: A body cell in metaphase of mitosis
column28: After meiosis I, each cell has 23 chromosomes (each still made of two chromatids), the same count as a gamete. A common mistake is thinking the number halves only at the end of meiosis II.
column29: Which division separates the homologous pairs and halves the count?

column9: Why is meiosis II often described as being 'like mitosis'?
column14: In both, sister chromatids are pulled apart and the chromosome number in each cell stays the same through that division
column15: Both make diploid cells
column17: Both begin by copying the DNA
column28: Like mitosis, meiosis II splits sister chromatids without changing the count per cell. The DNA is not copied again before meiosis II, which is the common mistake.
column29: Think about what separates in meiosis II and in mitosis.

column9: A doe's egg has 35 chromosomes, and a buck's sperm has 35. After fertilization, the zygote divides many times by mitosis. How many chromosomes are in each skin cell of the fawn?
column28: 35 + 35 = 70 in the zygote, and mitosis keeps that number in every body cell. A common mistake is halving again because cells divided; mitosis does not change the number.
column29: Add the gametes, then remember what mitosis does to the number.

column9: A student counts chromosomes in cells from a rat's testis. Some cells have 42 and some have 21. What is the best explanation?
column14: The 42-chromosome cells are germ or body cells, and the 21-chromosome cells are sperm made by meiosis
column15: The 21-chromosome cells are damaged and lost half their chromosomes
column17: The 21-chromosome cells were made by mitosis
column28: Rats are 2n = 42, so 21 is the haploid number of sperm made by meiosis. Mitosis would keep 42, which is the common mistake.
column29: Which number is diploid and which is haploid?

column9: Which statement about homologous chromosomes is correct?
column14: They carry the same genes, but may carry different versions (alleles) of those genes
column15: They are exact copies of each other
column16: They are made during the S phase
column28: Homologs have the same genes in the same order, but one came from each parent, so the alleles can differ. Exact copies made in S phase are sister chromatids, the common mix-up.
column29: One came from mom and one from dad. Would they be exactly the same?

column9: A lab group builds a bead model of meiosis for a cell with 2n = 6. At the end of meiosis II, how many chromosomes should be in each model cell?
column28: Each final cell is haploid: 6 ÷ 2 = 3. A common mistake is dividing by 4 because there are 4 cells; the number halves only once.
column29: The chromosome number is halved once, in meiosis I.

column9: A cell is shown with its chromosomes in homologous pairs, and the pairs are lined up across the middle. Which statements about this cell are true? Select all that apply.
column14: It is in metaphase I
column15: It is going through meiosis, not mitosis
column16: Its sister chromatids are about to separate
column17: Crossing over has already had a chance to happen
column28: Pairs at the middle means metaphase I of meiosis, after prophase I when crossing over happens. Next, the homologs separate, not the sister chromatids. The cell is still diploid. The sister chromatid choice is the common trap.
column29: What separates next, in anaphase I?

column9: A classmate says, "Meiosis is just mitosis done twice." What is the best correction?
column14: Meiosis I separates homologous pairs and halves the chromosome number; mitosis never separates homologous pairs
column15: Meiosis II copies the DNA again, so it is different
column16: Mitosis also makes four cells, so the classmate is partly right
column28: Meiosis I is unlike mitosis: homologous pairs separate and the number is halved. Only meiosis II is like mitosis. A common mistake is thinking DNA is copied again before meiosis II.
column29: Focus on what separates in meiosis I.

column9: A sheep has 54 chromosomes in its body cells. How many chromosomes are in one of its cells during metaphase II?
column28: Meiosis I already halved the number, so a cell in meiosis II has 54 ÷ 2 = 27. A common mistake is answering 54, thinking the number halves only at the very end.
column29: Has meiosis I happened yet in metaphase II?

column9: A human germ cell in a male and a human germ cell in a female each finish meiosis. How do their results compare?
column14: The male's makes four sperm; the female's makes one egg plus small polar bodies
column15: The male's makes one sperm; the female's makes four eggs
column16: Both make four gametes of equal size
column28: Sperm formation gives 4 sperm. Egg formation divides the cytoplasm unevenly, so one large egg forms and the small polar bodies break down. A common mistake is thinking a female makes four eggs at once.
column29: Egg cells are huge. Can a cell split into four huge cells?

column9: A class models meiosis with socks, where each matched pair of socks stands for a homologous pair. A drawer holds 4 pairs. To model one gamete, what should a student take out?
column14: One sock from each of the 4 pairs
column15: Both socks from 2 of the pairs
column17: Any 4 socks, even two from the same pair
column28: A gamete gets exactly one member of every homologous pair. Taking both socks of a pair would give the gamete two copies of some chromosomes and none of others, which is the common mistake.
column29: Every gamete needs one copy of every chromosome.

column9: Which comparison of a human sperm cell and a human egg cell is correct?
column14: Both are haploid with 23 chromosomes, but the egg is much larger
column15: The sperm has 23 chromosomes and the egg has 46
column17: The egg can carry a Y chromosome
column28: Both gametes have 23, so together they make 46. The egg is larger because it holds the cytoplasm the zygote needs. A common mistake is thinking the bigger egg has more chromosomes.
column29: A zygote has 46. How much must each gamete give?

column9: A sunflower has 34 chromosomes in its leaf cells. A sunflower sperm fertilizes a sunflower egg. How many chromosomes does the zygote have?
column28: Each gamete has 17, and 17 + 17 = 34. The zygote is diploid, like the leaf cells. A common mistake is adding 34 + 34 = 68, using the body-cell number for the gametes.
column29: First find the gamete number, then add two of them.

column9: Which part of meiosis is mainly responsible for making the cells haploid?
column14: Meiosis I, when homologous pairs separate
column15: Meiosis II, when sister chromatids separate
column17: Cytokinesis at the end of meiosis II
column28: Separating the homologous pairs in meiosis I sends one of each pair to each cell, so the cells become haploid. Meiosis II only splits sister chromatids, the common mistake.
column29: Which division splits up the pairs?

column9: An onion has 16 chromosomes in its body cells. One onion germ cell has just finished meiosis I. Which describes each of the two new cells?
column14: 8 chromosomes, each still made of two sister chromatids
column15: 8 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
column16: 16 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids
column28: Meiosis I separates homologs, so each cell has 8 chromosomes, but the sister chromatids are not split until meiosis II. A common mistake is thinking the chromatids also separate in meiosis I.
column29: Two things must be checked: the number of chromosomes, and whether the chromatids have split yet.

column9: A human germ cell is in prophase I. How many chromatids does it contain?
column28: The cell has 46 chromosomes, and each was copied into 2 sister chromatids: 46 × 2 = 92. A common mistake is answering 46, counting chromosomes instead of chromatids.
column29: The DNA was copied before meiosis started. How many chromatids does each chromosome have?

column9: A goat has 60 chromosomes in its body cells. How many chromatids are in one of its cells during metaphase II?
column28: In metaphase II the cell has 30 chromosomes (halved in meiosis I), and each still has 2 chromatids: 30 × 2 = 60. A common mistake is answering 30, forgetting the chromatids haven't split yet.
column29: First find the chromosome number after meiosis I, then count chromatids per chromosome.

column9: A tomato egg cell holds 1 unit of DNA. How many units of DNA does a tomato germ cell hold at the start of prophase I?
column28: A diploid cell has 2 units (double the egg), and copying DNA in S phase doubles it to 4 before meiosis I. A common mistake is answering 2, forgetting that DNA is copied before meiosis begins.
column29: Go from haploid to diploid, then remember what S phase does.

column9: A mule is born when a horse (2n = 64) and a donkey (2n = 62) mate. Mules are almost always sterile. What is the best explanation?
column14: Its chromosomes cannot all form matching homologous pairs in meiosis I, so it cannot make normal gametes
column15: It has too few chromosomes to do mitosis
column28: Half the mule's chromosomes are from a horse and half from a donkey, and they do not match up well, so meiosis I fails. Mitosis works fine, which is why mules grow normally; blaming mitosis is the common mistake.
column29: Meiosis I depends on chromosomes finding a matching partner.

column9: A horse's body cells have 64 chromosomes and a donkey's have 62. How many chromosomes are in a mule's body cells?
column28: Horse gamete 64 ÷ 2 = 32, donkey gamete 62 ÷ 2 = 31, and 32 + 31 = 63. A common mistake is adding the body-cell numbers, 64 + 62 = 126.
column29: Find each parent's gamete number first, then add.

column9: During meiosis in a man, the X and Y chromosomes fail to separate, so one sperm ends up with only 22 chromosomes and no sex chromosome. If it fertilizes a normal egg, how many chromosomes will the zygote have?
column28: 22 + 23 = 45. This failure to separate is called nondisjunction, and a zygote with one X and no second sex chromosome has Turner syndrome. A common mistake is assuming the zygote always gets 46.
column29: Add the sperm's number to the egg's number.

column9: In anaphase I, one homologous pair fails to separate and both chromosomes go to the same cell. Meiosis II then happens normally. What is true of the four gametes?
column14: All four have the wrong number of chromosomes
column15: Only one gamete is affected
column16: All four are normal because meiosis II fixes the mistake
column17: Two are normal and two are abnormal
column28: One cell from meiosis I has an extra chromosome and the other is missing one, so both of its daughters in meiosis II are affected too: two n + 1 and two n − 1. A common mistake is thinking only one gamete is affected.
column29: Follow both cells from meiosis I into meiosis II.

column9: A student's drawing of human meiosis shows two cells with 23 chromosomes after meiosis I, then four cells with 11 or 12 chromosomes after meiosis II. What did the student get wrong?
column14: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, so each final cell should still have 23
column15: Meiosis I should leave 46 chromosomes in each cell
column16: There should be 8 cells at the end
column17: Nothing; the number halves in both divisions
column28: The number halves once, in meiosis I. Meiosis II splits chromatids, so 23 stays 23. The common mistake is halving twice because there are two divisions.
column29: What separates in meiosis II, and does that change the chromosome count?

column9: A cell has 2n = 4: a long pair (L1 from mom, L2 from dad) and a short pair (S1 from mom, S2 from dad). Ignoring crossing over, which chromosome sets could be in one of its gametes? Select all that apply.
column14: L1 and S1
column15: L1 and S2
column28: A gamete gets one long and one short chromosome, in any mix: L1S1, L1S2, L2S1, L2S2. L1 with L2 (or S1 with S2) puts both members of one pair in a gamete, the common mistake.
column29: Every gamete needs one from each pair.

column9: An organism has 2n = 10. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can independent assortment produce?
column28: There are 5 pairs, each with 2 ways to line up: 2⁵ = 32. A common mistake is using 2¹⁰ with the diploid number, or 2 × 5 = 10.
column29: Find the number of pairs, then raise 2 to that power.

column9: In a species with 2n = 4, a mother and a father can each make 4 kinds of gametes (ignoring crossing over). How many different chromosome combinations are possible in the zygotes of their offspring?
column28: Any of the 4 egg types can meet any of the 4 sperm types: 4 × 4 = 16. A common mistake is adding (4 + 4 = 8) instead of multiplying.
column29: Make a table with egg types on one side and sperm types on the other.

column9: If crossing over never happened, which statement would be true?
column14: Gametes could still differ because of independent assortment
column15: Every gamete from one person would be identical
column28: Without crossing over, the random line-up of pairs in metaphase I still gives millions of combinations. A common mistake is thinking crossing over is the only source of variation.
column29: There are two ways meiosis shuffles genes. Take one away.

column9: Put these descriptions of a cell going through meiosis in order.
column14: Four cells, each with one set of single, unduplicated chromosomes
column15: Homologous pairs lined up across the middle of one cell
column16: Two cells, each with duplicated chromosomes lined up single file
column17: Homologous chromosomes pairing up and crossing over in one cell
column18: Two cells forming, each with one duplicated chromosome from every pair
column28: Prophase I (pair and cross over) → metaphase I (pairs at the middle) → telophase I (two cells) → metaphase II (single file) → end of meiosis II (four cells). A common mistake is putting the single-file line-up before the cell has split in two.
column29: Look at the number of cells in each description first: one, then two, then four.

column9: An organism has 2n = 6. Under a microscope, a cell shows 3 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids, lined up single file at the middle. Which phase is it in?
column14: Metaphase I
column15: Metaphase II
column28: Only 3 chromosomes means the cell is already haploid, and single file with chromatids still attached is metaphase II. Metaphase I and mitosis would both show all 6, which is the common trap.
column29: Is the cell haploid or diploid? That tells you whether meiosis I is done.

column9: An organism has 2n = 8. A cell is seen with single chromatids being pulled toward each pole, 4 toward one pole and 4 toward the other. Which phase is it in?
column14: Anaphase I
column15: Anaphase II
column28: Single chromatids moving means sister chromatids are separating, and only 4 per pole means the cell is haploid: anaphase II. Anaphase of mitosis would send 8 to each pole, and anaphase I moves duplicated chromosomes, the common traps.
column29: Ask two questions: are sister chromatids separating, and how many go to each pole?

column9: A new fungus attacks a population of plants. Why might a population that reproduces sexually have a better chance of surviving than one that only reproduces asexually?
column14: Meiosis and fertilization create genetic variation, so some offspring may have traits that resist the fungus
column15: Sexual reproduction always makes more offspring
column17: Sexually produced plants are identical, so they all resist the fungus
column28: Variation from meiosis means some individuals may survive a new threat. Asexual offspring are copies, so if one is vulnerable they all are. A common mistake is thinking sexual offspring are identical.
column29: Which population has more differences among its members?

column9: Which statement correctly compares homologous chromosomes and sister chromatids?
column14: Homologous chromosomes come from different parents and may carry different alleles; sister chromatids are copies made in S phase and start out identical
column15: Both are identical copies made in S phase
column16: Homologous chromosomes are made in S phase; sister chromatids come from different parents
column17: Sister chromatids separate in meiosis I; homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis II
column28: Homologs are a mom-and-dad pair. Sister chromatids are two copies of one chromosome. Homologs separate in meiosis I and chromatids in meiosis II; flipping those is the common mistake.
column29: Which pair came from two parents, and which was made by copying?

column9: An alligator egg cell has 16 chromosomes. It is fertilized by a normal sperm, and the zygote divides by mitosis three times. How many chromosomes are in each of the resulting cells?
column28: 16 + 16 = 32 in the zygote, and mitosis keeps 32 in every cell, no matter how many times it divides. A common mistake is halving with each division or multiplying by 8 cells.
column29: Find the zygote number, then ask what mitosis does to it.

column9: A student claims, "Crossing over makes brand-new genes." What is the best response?
column14: Crossing over moves existing versions of genes between homologous chromosomes into new combinations; it does not create new genes
column15: That is correct; each crossover writes a new gene
column16: Crossing over adds new chromosomes to the cell
column17: Crossing over happens only in mitosis, so it cannot affect genes
column28: Crossing over trades matching segments, so the same genes end up in new combinations of alleles. New versions of genes come from mutations, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Were the pieces that got swapped already there?

column9: In a human male, which of these cells contain a Y chromosome? Select all that apply.
column14: A skin cell
column15: A germ cell in the testis before meiosis
column17: About half of his sperm cells
column18: Both cells at the end of meiosis I
column28: Body cells and germ cells are XY. In meiosis I, the X and Y separate, so one cell gets the Y and the other gets the X, and about half the sperm carry Y. Thinking every sperm has a Y is the common mistake.
column29: When do the X and Y separate?

column9: A rabbit has 2n = 44. A germ cell in a female rabbit's ovary finished meiosis and formed one large cell and three tiny cells. What are the tiny cells, and how many chromosomes does each have?
column14: Polar bodies, each with 22 chromosomes
column15: Sperm cells, each with 22 chromosomes
column28: Egg formation splits the cytoplasm unevenly. The tiny cells are polar bodies, and like the egg they are haploid (22). A common mistake is thinking polar bodies keep the diploid number.
column29: All four cells came from meiosis. What is their chromosome number?

column9: Which human cell contains the most DNA?
column14: A germ cell in prophase I
column15: A cell at the end of meiosis I
column17: A skin cell before its DNA is copied
column28: In prophase I, all 46 chromosomes are copied (4 units if a sperm has 1). The end of meiosis I has 2 units, an unreplicated skin cell has 2, and a sperm has 1. A common mistake is ignoring the DNA copying before meiosis.
column29: Which cell is diploid AND has already copied its DNA?

column9: An organism has 2n = 8. One of its cells is in anaphase I. How many chromosomes are moving toward each pole?
column28: In anaphase I, the homologous pairs split, so each pole gets one chromosome from each of the 4 pairs. A common mistake is answering 8 by counting chromatids or thinking it is mitosis.
column29: In anaphase I, the pairs separate. How many pairs are there?

column9: A woman's chromosome 5 pair carries gene version A on one chromosome and a on the other. Her chromosome 9 pair carries B on one and b on the other. Ignoring crossing over, what fraction of her eggs will carry both A and B?
column28: Half her eggs get A, and because the pairs sort independently, half of those also get B: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. A common mistake is answering 1/2 by looking at only one gene.
column29: Find the chance for A, then the chance for B, and multiply.
